chunks: From him, from Ali ibn Ri'ab and Abdullah ibn Jabalah, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, from 'Abd al-Salih (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a man who has a house in his possession that does not belong to him, and it has remained in his hand and the hand of his fathers before him. Those of his fathers who passed away knew that it did not belong to them, but they did not know to whom it belonged, so he sells it and takes its price. He (the Imam) said: 'I do not like that he sells what does not belong to him.' I said: 'Indeed, he does not know its owner, nor does he know to whom it belongs, and I do not think its master will ever come.' He said: 'I do not like that he sells what does not belong to him.' I said: 'Then he sells its usufruct (residency right) or its location in his hand, so he says to its owner: I sell you my residency, and it will be in your hand as it is in my hand.' He said: 'Yes, he sells it on this basis.'
ai.seo_question: Can a person sell a property they possess but do not own if the true owner is unknown?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Shia juristic distinction between *al-ayn* (the physical property) and *al-manfa'ah* (the usufruct), resolving the ambiguity of *gharar* in transactions involving unknown owners. Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that while selling the asset itself is disliked due to potential ownership claims, selling the right of residence is permissible, reflecting a pragmatic approach to preserving economic utility while minimizing risk. This ruling underscores the principle that uncertainty in the object's identity does not invalidate the contract if the right being transferred is clearly defined and possessed.
